name: Clear aligners

lead: Clear aligners are a series of removable, transparent plastic trays, each shaped slightly differently, that move teeth step by step into a planned position. They straighten crowded or spaced teeth and correct some bite problems, with the appeal of being far less visible than metal braces.

A digital scan is used to plan the movements, and each tray applies light force that remodels the bone around the tooth roots. Invisalign began US sales in 1999, and many dentist-supervised and direct-to-consumer systems now exist. Reviews describe aligners as best suited to mild to moderate crowding or spacing, with a 2022 review putting tooth-movement accuracy against prediction at around 50 percent.

paras: Trays are worn about 22 hours a day, each for one to two weeks, and treatment runs for months, usually followed by retainers. A dentist or orthodontist makes the plan and checks progress.

Aligners are less predictable for rotations, extrusion and root control. Risks include gum recession, root resorption, relapse without retainers and poor outcomes when worn too little. Mail-order versions omit in-person supervision, and larger jaw problems are generally described as needing other treatment.

angle.text: Users wear clear aligners to straighten teeth and correct bite, which improves the smile and how the lower face looks. Tooth movement is well studied; claims about jaw or facial-skeleton change are limited and debated.

lead: Clear aligners are removable, transparent plastic orthodontic trays that straighten teeth in small steps, and people use them to improve the look of their smile and dental alignment without the visible metal of conventional braces. A digital scan or impression is used to plan the movements in software, and each tray is shaped slightly differently from the last. A tray is typically worn for one to two weeks and for about 22 hours a day. [1] Straighter, better-spaced teeth change how the lower face reads in smiling and speaking, which is why aligners are a common first step in appearance-focused dental work. [2]

Align Technology's Invisalign, with US sales beginning in 1999, is the best-known system; many other brands, including dentist-supervised and direct-to-consumer (DTC) mail-order services, have followed. [1][3][4] Aligners are used to correct crowded or spaced teeth and some bite problems, with the appeal that they are far less visible than metal braces and can be taken out for eating and cleaning. [1][2] Wikipedia describes them as indicated mainly for mild to moderate crowding or spacing of roughly 1 to 6 mm in cases without jaw discrepancies, and as likely less effective than conventional braces for some movements such as rotations. [1]

The research literature includes many systematic reviews, and their conclusions are qualified. A 2015 systematic review identified methodological shortcomings in the available studies, and later reviews and meta-analyses compare aligners with fixed appliances across malocclusion types, in adults and in extraction cases. [5][6][7] A 2022 review stated that tooth-movement accuracy relative to prediction was around 50 percent. [8] Orthodontic organisations including the American Association of Orthodontists have raised concerns about DTC services that lack in-person dentist supervision, and the best-known DTC company, SmileDirectClub, ceased operations in December 2023. [1][9]

On forums such as looksmax.org, aligners are discussed as an option for people who want straighter teeth and wonder how they compare with braces for facial structure, gum recession, palate shape and overbite. [10][11][12][13]
infobox: Removable orthodontic appliance (series of thermoformed trays) [1]
Invisalign (Align Technology); company founded 1997, US sales from 1999 [1][18]
About 22 hours a day, tray changed every 1-2 weeks [1]
Dentist or orthodontist; direct-to-consumer variants have existed [1]

paras: Treatment begins with diagnostic x-rays and photographs and capture of the bite and teeth by impressions or an intraoral scanner, and the dentist or orthodontist writes a treatment plan. A technician or software moves the teeth virtually through intermediate stages, and a digital preview, in Align's system called ClinCheck, is shown to the clinician and patient for approval before aligners are made. [1] Bonded composite attachments are often added to teeth to help the plastic grip and produce particular movements, and a 2022 systematic review examined the effect of composite attachments on aligner therapy. [1][14]

A 2023 review lists the advantages of clear aligner therapy as near invisibility, comfort and removability for eating and brushing, and notes that Invisalign was initially available only to orthodontists but was later extended to general dentists. [2] A 2017 review noted at least 27 different clear aligner products on offer. [3] The material and design of aligners have been reviewed in the bioengineering literature. [15] Biomechanical studies have measured the forces and moments generated by aligners for incisor torque, premolar derotation and molar distalization. [16]

Wikipedia reports that each aligner moves teeth roughly 0.25 to 0.33 mm, so a full case involves a long series of trays, and that hot liquids can warp aligners and a retainer is advised after treatment. [1] Grokipedia adds that trays are usually thermoformed plastics such as polyurethane or PETG, about 0.5 to 1 mm thick, and that tiny amounts of enamel between teeth are sometimes removed (interproximal reduction) to create space. [4] After active treatment, retainers are standard in orthodontics because teeth can relapse; Wikipedia's orthodontics article says more than half of patients show some reversion within ten years. [17]

A 2017 review traces removable appliances analogous to clear aligners to the Tooth Positioner introduced in 1944, with modern clear aligner therapy becoming widespread after Invisalign's introduction in 1998. [3] Wikipedia says Align Technology was founded in 1997 by Zia Chishti, who conceived the idea as an adult orthodontic patient wearing a retainer; sales began in the US in 1999, orthodontists were initially resistant, and by 2014 some 80,000 dentists had been trained to use the system. [1] The Align Technology article adds that the company was co-founded with Kelsey Wirth, that the FDA cleared the product in 1998, and that a 2000 New York Times report described a planned $31 million television campaign as the most aggressive consumer advertising plan the dental profession had seen. [18][19]

Align went public on Nasdaq on 26 January 2001 and raised about $130 million. A 2001 class-action suit alleged that limiting Invisalign to orthodontists was unfair to general dentists, after which it was opened to them. Thomas Prescott replaced Chishti as chief executive in 2002, the company first turned a profit in 2003, and revenue passed $1 billion in 2016. Its first patents began expiring in October 2017, opening the market to competitors. [18]

Chishti left Align and developed a competing product, OrthoClear, in 2005, leading to patent and other legal disputes that were settled in 2006 with Align paying OrthoClear $20 million and OrthoClear ceasing operations. Dentist Willis Pumphrey founded ClearCorrect in 2006; Inc. magazine named it the fastest-growing health company in America in 2011, and Straumann acquired it in 2017. [1] In 2009 Align began requiring Invisalign providers to treat at least ten cases a year and complete training, and about 20,000 doctors had their certification suspended in January 2010, though a class action restored some. [1]

SmileDirectClub was founded in Nashville, Tennessee in 2014 by Jordan Katzman and Alex Fenkell. Customers took impressions at home and licensed dentists or orthodontists supervised treatment remotely; the company also ran about 300 retail locations. It raised $380 million at a reported $3.2 billion valuation in October 2018, expanded to Canada, the UK and Australia, and listed on Nasdaq on 12 September 2019. [9] It had begun as a distributor of Align's aligners, and a later dispute led to a 2021 arbitration award of $43.4 million plus interest to Align. [9]

The American Association of Orthodontists filed complaints with 36 state dental boards, and a class action filed in September 2019 alleged false advertising and FDA violations. A January 2020 New York Times report described the company's use of non-disclosure agreements about customer complaints, and a March 2020 CBC Marketplace hidden-camera investigation found all four undercover patients were approved for treatment, though orthodontists said none should have been. The company responded with changes to training and forms and disputed several of the claims, and it sued NBC News over a report on complaints, a suit dismissed in December 2021 under Tennessee's anti-SLAPP law. [9] The company filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy on 29 September 2023, ceased operations on 8 December 2023 and was converted to Chapter 7 in January 2024; its assets and technology were acquired by SmileSet. [9]

Other DTC and mail-order services have continued, and Wikipedia notes that Dentsply Sirona voluntarily suspended sales and marketing of its Byte aligners and impression kits in October 2024 while reviewing regulatory requirements. [1] Grokipedia reports that at least eight US states require an in-person exam before aligner therapy and that DTC prices around $2,000 compare with several thousand dollars for professionally managed systems. [4] The American Association of Orthodontists has issued a consumer alert about mail-order services. [1]

A 2015 systematic review found 11 relevant studies and highlighted methodological shortcomings, and Wikipedia notes that a 2014 review concluded the published evidence was insufficient to determine effectiveness. [1][5] An earlier prospective study of 37 patients measured predicted versus achieved movement of 401 anterior teeth, and a 2020 follow-up study of 38 patients using intraoral scans examined whether accuracy had improved. [20][21] A 2014 study of 30 patients examined incisor torque, premolar derotation and molar distalization and the influence of attachments and staging. [22]

Systematic reviews of effectiveness include an Invisalign-focused review in 2018, a 2020 review of clear aligner therapy, and a 2017 meta-analysis of efficiency, effectiveness and stability. [23][24][25] A 2023 systematic review compared aligners with fixed appliances in complicated and severe malocclusions, a 2025 systematic review compared them for anterior teeth in adults, and a 2025 meta-analysis compared effectiveness across malocclusion types. [26][27][7] A 2019 comparative study and a 2005 outcome assessment using the American Board of Orthodontics grading system compared aligner and traditional treatment results. [28][29] A 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis examined aligners in extraction-based treatment. [6]

A 2022 review on biomechanics argued that accuracy of tooth movement versus prediction was around 50 percent, and described vigorous advertising of aligners to patients and clinicians on social media. [8] Wikipedia reports that aligners are generally considered useful for moderate front-tooth crowding and that relapse of anterior teeth has been found more frequently than with conventional braces. [1]

Grokipedia cites figures for aligner suitability, including a typical indication of crowding or spacing up to about 6 mm and reported compliance data in which about 36 percent of patients wore trays the full recommended time, and describes refinements (additional tray sets) as common; it is an AI-generated source and the figures vary across studies. [4] Wikipedia's orthodontics article says there is insufficient evidence on aligner effectiveness while noting some people regard them as faster and less restrictive. [17]

Controlled trials include a randomized trial of 40 adults with anterior open bite comparing clear aligners with fixed appliances plus miniscrews for molar intrusion, measuring root resorption, intrusion and bite force at six months. [30] A randomized trial compared Invisalign First phase I treatment with tooth-borne rapid maxillary expansion in mixed-dentition patients for palatal volume and surface area. [31] A randomized trial compared periodontal health and quality of life with aligners versus fixed appliances after orthognathic surgery, and another randomized trial compared finished case quality between Invisalign and fixed appliances. [32][33] A 2006 clinical trial examined finishing with Invisalign, and a randomized trial examined clear aligners and sleep bruxism. [34][35] An editorial discussed the transparency of Invisalign. [36]

The reviews cited above point to variable predictability for certain tooth movements. Reported risks in the literature include relapse after treatment, root resorption, which one trial measured in aligner and fixed-appliance molar intrusion, and gum and periodontal effects, which another trial assessed after orthognathic surgery. [1][30][32] Outcomes depend on wear time, and aligners are removable. [1][2] Wikipedia notes that aligners are not recommended for children in conventional use, and the American Association of Orthodontists issued a consumer alert about direct-to-consumer services lacking in-person supervision. [1]

In the United States clear aligners are regulated as FDA Class II medical devices, according to Grokipedia, and the FDA warned Align in 2010 according to a reference in Wikipedia's Align article. [4][18] Wikipedia's article on orthodontics lists decalcification and tooth decay as the main complications of fixed braces with poor hygiene, a risk profile that differs from removable trays. [17] Grokipedia reports root resorption of 1 to 2 mm in a minority of cases and temporary lisps that typically settle within one to two weeks. [4]

Wikipedia reports that prices in Australia, Canada, the United States and the United Kingdom are fairly similar across providers at about $2,000 or 1,500 pounds, and that aligners are typically less costly than all-metal braces; the exact cost depends on the treatment plan, age, location and clinician. [1]

Grokipedia reports insurance coverage of often 25 to 50 percent of orthodontic costs, and describes DTC pricing of around $995 to $2,000 compared with $5,000 to $8,000 for professional systems in the US. [4]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, clear aligners are discussed as an alternative to braces, with recurring questions about gum recession, palate expansion, overbite and jaw position, and about whether aligners address skeletal problems. Posters also compare DTC and in-person options.[10][11][12][13]

claims.claim: Braces cause gum recession, so Invisalign is the safer choice for facial structure.
Invisalign can expand the palate slightly while straightening teeth.
Aligners alone cannot fix a larger overbite, which needs a Herbst or Forsus appliance.
Aligners (or braces) will not fix a recessed jaw or maxilla, so surgery is needed.
Mail-order aligners give the same result as an orthodontist at half the price.
Aligners are faster and less hassle than braces.
A retainer is needed after aligners or the teeth move back.
